learn: Five questions that classify any RL algorithm
The Bellman recursion as the thread linking DP, TD, DQN and actor–critic
Keeping state, reward, return and value distinct
From bandits to TD control in one view, with a worked TD error
Approximation, deep value learning and policy gradients in one update form
A checklist for formulating a new problem
intro.why: After many algorithms, the goal is a map: knowing which design choices separate methods lets you choose, combine and debug them, and formulate new problems well before writing any code.

sections.title: Five questions that classify any method
sections.plain: What does it learn, where do its targets come from, does it use a model, does it bootstrap, how is data generated?
sections.body:
The subject answered one question (how should an agent learn to make a sequence of decisions when actions influence what happens next?) in layers: bandits, finite MDPs, dynamic programming, Monte Carlo, TD, function approximation, deep value learning, policy optimisation, model-based planning and extensions. Algorithms differ mainly in five choices:

  1. What is learned: state values, action values, a policy, a model, or several.
  2. Where targets come from: expected backups (model), sampled full returns, bootstrapped one-step or n-step targets.
  3. Model use: none, a given model, or a learned model.
  4. Bootstrapping: does the target use current estimates?
  5. Data generation: on-policy, off-policy (any behaviour, logged data, replay), simulated.

sections.title: The Bellman thread
sections.plain: Long-term value is the immediate reward plus the discounted value of what follows, everywhere.
sections.body:
$$v_\pi(s) = \mathbb E_\pi[R_{t+1} + \gamma v_\pi(S_{t+1})\mid S_t=s],\qquad q_*(s,a) = \mathbb E\big[R_{t+1} + \gamma\max_{a'}q_*(S_{t+1},a')\mid s,a\big]$$

DP uses the recursion with a known model; TD and Q-learning with sampled transitions; DQN replaces the table with a network; actor–critic uses a value estimate learned this way to guide a parameterised policy; planning applies it to simulated experience. The form changes; the recursion stays.

sections.title: State, reward, return and value
sections.plain: Situation, one-step signal, realised total, expected total.
sections.body:
• State $S_t$: describes the situation (ideally Markov).
  • Reward $R_{t+1}$: one immediate scalar signal.
  • Return $G_t = \sum_k\gamma^kR_{t+k+1}$: a random, realised accumulation of future rewards in one trajectory.
  • Value $v_\pi(s) = \mathbb E_\pi[G_t\mid S_t=s]$: the expected return under a policy.

Most RL confusions come from mixing these: maximising immediate reward instead of value; treating one episode's return as the value; or forgetting that values depend on the policy.

sections.title: From bandits to TD control
sections.plain: Exploration in bandits, planning with DP, sampling with MC, bootstrapping with TD.
sections.body:
Bandits isolate exploration vs exploitation with no state transitions (ε-greedy, optimistic initial values, UCB, gradient bandits). Dynamic programming plans with a known model (policy/value iteration, GPI). Monte Carlo learns from complete sampled returns: no model, no bootstrap. TD updates after one transition and bootstraps: $\delta_t = R_{t+1} + \gamma V(S_{t+1}) - V(S_t)$. SARSA (on-policy), Q-learning (off-policy greedy target) and Expected SARSA differ only in the next-action part of their target.

Worked. $R_{t+1} = 2$, γ = 0.9, $V(S_t) = 1.0$, $V(S_{t+1}) = 1.5$: $\delta_t = 2 + 0.9(1.5) - 1.0 = 2.35$. The same number can drive a value update (critic, e.g. 1.0 → 1.235 with α = 0.1) and scale a policy-score update (actor).

Code example ex2 runs five methods on the same maze with the same budget: over episodes 21–30, Dyna-Q (10 planning steps) averages 16.9 steps (optimum 14), Q-learning and Expected SARSA 23.5, MC control 22.8, SARSA 29.7.

sections.title: Approximation, deep value and direct policy
sections.plain: Replace tables with functions; stabilise deep Q-learning; or optimise the policy directly.
sections.body:
Tabular methods fail when states are numerous or continuous. Function approximation replaces the table with $\hat v(s,\mathbf w) = \mathbf w^\top\mathbf x(s)$ or a network (semi-gradient TD; beware the deadly triad). DQN stabilises deep Q-learning with experience replay, a target network and learned features; Double DQN fixes maximisation bias.

Policy-gradient methods optimise $\pi_\theta$ directly with one reusable form:

$$\Delta\theta \propto (\text{quality signal});\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(A_t\mid S_t)$$

where the quality signal is the return (REINFORCE), the advantage (with a baseline), or the TD error/GAE (actor–critic); PPO reuses a fresh batch via the clipped ratio; RLHF, DPO and GRPO adapt this to language models.

sections.title: Three classifications to keep separate
sections.plain: Model-based or not, value- or policy-based, on- or off-policy: independent questions.
sections.body:
• Model-based vs model-free: is a model used to predict or simulate?
  • Value-based vs policy-based: does the action rule come from values (argmax) or from a parameterised policy?
  • On-policy vs off-policy: does learning target the policy that generated the data?

They combine freely: DQN is value-based and off-policy (model-free); PPO is policy-based and on-policy (with a value critic); MCTS is model-based decision-time planning; SAC is off-policy actor–critic; Dyna-Q is model-based, value-based, off-policy.

The historical progression: DP → MC → TD → function approximation → DQN / actor–critic → modern extensions (PPO, RLHF, model-based planning, multi-agent and safe RL).

sections.title: How to model a new problem
sections.plain: Define the interface first: agents, state, actions, reward, horizon, data, model, output, constraints, evaluation.
sections.body:
A good solution starts with the interface, not the network. Before choosing an algorithm, decide:

  1. the agent(s);
  2. the state or observation (is it Markov?);
  3. the action space (discrete, continuous, structured);
  4. the reward or other feedback (goal, not method; preferences? demonstrations?);
  5. the horizon and true terminal states;
  6. the data source: free simulation, logged data, or expensive real interaction;
  7. whether a model is available or learnable;
  8. the required output (policy, value estimate, plan);
  9. constraints (safety, budgets, fairness);
  10. evaluation measures beyond return (violations, robustness, human review).

The answers largely determine the algorithm: discrete actions + cheap simulation → DQN or PPO; continuous control with expensive data → SAC/TD3 with replay; logged data only → off-policy evaluation and offline RL; known rules → search (MCTS); preferences → RLHF/DPO.

sections.title: Further insights and misconceptions
sections.body:
• Most failures are formulation failures: non-Markov states, mis-specified rewards, truncation treated as termination, or evaluation on the training reward alone.
  • Baselines first: compare against simple heuristics and tabular or linear methods before scaling up.
  • Reproducibility: RL results vary greatly across seeds; report several seeds with confidence intervals.
  • Where to go next: offline RL, hierarchical RL, meta-RL, exploration bonuses, and RL for reasoning in language models.

code.title: One TD error, many uses
code.explain: Computes δ = 2.35, uses it for a critic and an actor update, shows how SARSA, Expected SARSA, Q-learning and TD(0) targets differ for the same transition, and compares quality signals in the unified policy-update form.
mistakes: Using the TD error from a stale critic for the actor.
Mixing up the next-action term between methods.
code.notes: One number, two roles: critic learning and actor credit.
code.code:
"""One TD error, many uses: the same number drives a critic, an actor, and differs by target choice.

R = 2, gamma = 0.9, V(S) = 1.0, V(S') = 1.5.
"""
import numpy as np
R, g, V, V2 = 2.0, 0.9, 1.0, 1.5
delta = R + g * V2 - V
print(f"TD error: {R} + {g}*{V2} - {V} = {delta:.2f}")
print(f"critic update (alpha_w = 0.1): V(S) = {V} + 0.1*{delta:.2f} = {V + 0.1 * delta:.3f}")
th = np.array([0.0, 0.0]); pi = np.exp(th) / np.exp(th).sum(); score = np.array([1, 0]) - pi
print(f"actor update (alpha = 0.1, action 0 taken): theta = {np.round(th + 0.1 * delta * score, 4)} -> pi = "
      f"{np.round(np.exp(th + 0.1 * delta * score) / np.exp(th + 0.1 * delta * score).sum(), 4)}")

Qn = {"left": 1.2, "right": 1.5}; taken = "left"; pi_next = {"left": 0.5, "right": 0.5}
targets = {"SARSA (next action taken)": R + g * Qn[taken], "Expected SARSA (50/50)": R + g * sum(pi_next[a] * Qn[a] for a in Qn),
           "Q-learning (max)": R + g * max(Qn.values()), "TD(0) on V": R + g * V2}
print("\nSame transition, next-action part of the target differs:")
for k, v in targets.items(): print(f"  {k:<28} target = {v:.3f}")

print("\nUnified policy-update form: delta_theta ~ (quality signal) * grad log pi")
for name, sig in [("REINFORCE: return G", 4.2), ("with baseline: G - b(s)", 4.2 - 3.0), ("actor-critic: TD error", delta)]:
    print(f"  {name:<26} signal = {sig:+.2f}")
